schema.name: contextual-anonymizer-cue-schema
schema.description: Annotation schema for detecting re-identifying cues in psychotherapy transcripts, covering both explicit identifiers and the implicit contextual cues that let a clinician recognise a patient without any identifier being present.
schema.provenance: Derived from five semi-structured clinician interviews conducted for the Contextual Anonymizer project.
schema.example_disclaimer: All examples in this file are synthetic and illustrative. They are constructed to demonstrate the code, not reproduced from any real session or interview. No example refers to an actual patient.
schema.typical_semantics: typical gives the prior RANGE for risk and nuance - the span the class plausibly occupies. The instance value is set by the scenario and by bundling; movers name what pushes it up or down. Ranges are deliberately not tuned as precise numbers: a range is a prior honest about being a prior. Example annotations show single instance values, normally inside the range; a value outside it needs a rationale.

changelog.0.4: 2026-08-31: NVB-LANG (code-switching) added as a marker-capable cue (tag_count 40 -> 41). Behaves like silence: harmless alone, raw material for bindings. Per-marker binding parameters added to anonymization-policy.json; detection becomes meaningful once non-English text enters the corpus.
changelog.0.3: 2026-08-31: typical priors become [lo, hi] ranges with a movers note per code (revised case-6 verdict: a range is the honest shape of a prior; tuning exact values stays evidence-driven).
changelog.0.2: 2026-08-24 jury round: KEEP-REL added (tag_count 39 -> 40); NAR-THIRD narrowed to identifying fragments with its treatment ladder; marker_capable flags on NVB-BODY/VOICE/SILENCE and INT-RESIST; NVB-BOUND binding numbers moved to anonymization-policy.json; rewrite_constraints on NAR-VERB/RARE/IDIOM (experiment-gated); participant policy, record reference and typical_semantics added; annotator rule 6 tightened to nuance >= 2.

record_reference: Span records serialise with the fields of Anon.md Appendix A plus later additions: transcript_id, span_id, utterance_id, char_start, char_end, speaker, annotator, adjudicated, release_tier, marker, bundle_ids, and a per-participant consent flag. The full object model (Document, Utterance, Span, Link, Bundle, Decision, Edit) is specified in docs/text-system-v0.md section 4. Actions are decided by the policy file (anonymization-policy.json); examples in this file show outcomes under policy v0.

annotation_unit.primary: character-offset span within a single utterance
annotation_unit.secondary: bundle, a set of spans across the transcript that are jointly identifying
annotation_unit.note: A span carries exactly one cue sub-code but may belong to several bundles. Overlapping labels on the same stretch of text are capped at two: one primary (what it mainly is) and one optional secondary (what else it carries). When more compete, choose the best two; if a phrase seems to need a third, split the phrase into smaller spans instead of stacking deeper.
annotation_unit.participant_policy: Everyone in the room is treated as a patient unless they are the therapist. Every participant - patient, companion, relative - gets patient-grade protection: their own fact-sheet, coreference and surrogate cluster, bundles, and consent flag. The therapist is an exception of purpose, not protection: clinician material (the CLI codes) is itself a research object, handled via the access-tier mechanism.

risk.definition: 0 none, 1 common attribute, 2 quasi-identifier, 3 singular or near-singular

rarity.definition: Annotator estimate of population frequency; feeds the selectivity table used by the risk model.

linkability.definition: internal means recognisable only to someone who knows the patient; external means matchable against a public source such as electoral rolls, professional networks, news or institutional directories.

nuance.definition: Clinical or cultural meaning lost if the span is removed. 3 means removal changes the clinical picture.

verbatim.definition: True if this is the patient's own wording rather than a clinician paraphrase.

bundle_ids.definition: Bundles this span participates in. Empty when the span is identifying on its own or not identifying at all.

action.definition: Derived from decision_matrix; overridable with a recorded reason in notes.

gen_level.definition: If GENERALISE, how far up the hierarchy to climb.

surrogate_key.definition: Coreference cluster key, ensuring one surrogate is applied at every mention across the transcript.

notes.definition: Required whenever action is overridden or the span was adjudicated.

risk_model.formula: k_hat(B) = N * PRODUCT over c in B of (s_c ^ w_c)

terms.N: size of the reference population, fixed by the threat model
terms.s_c: selectivity of cue c, the estimated fraction of the reference population retaining that attribute, in (0, 1]
terms.w_c: redundancy weight in (0, 1], discounting cues statistically dependent on another cue already in the bundle

risk_model.caveat: N is undefined until the threat model is fixed. Every threshold above inherits that choice.

decision_matrix.note: The risk 3 / nuance 3 cell is the whole project. Getting it wrong either leaks patients or returns transcripts with the clinical content hollowed out, and both failures score well on conventional precision and recall.

cue_classes.name: Direct identifiers
cue_classes.description: The conventional safe-harbor identifier set. Handled by an existing NER and rules layer, included here so the schema is complete and so annotators have somewhere to put these spans.

sub_codes.name: Personal name
sub_codes.description: Name of the patient, a relative, or any other individual.
sub_codes.movers: essentially fixed - a name is a name

example.text: My name is Ramesh Kulkarni and I am here about my sleep.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: Ramesh Kulkarni
example.after: My name is [NAME-01] and I am here about my sleep.

sub_codes.name: Geography below state level
sub_codes.description: Address, locality, town, postal code.
sub_codes.movers: address precision raises risk; status-bearing places shade toward DEM-SES

example.text: We stay in Sector 14, near the old water tank.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: Sector 14, near the old water tank
example.after: We stay in [LOCALITY-01], near a local landmark.

sub_codes.name: Date finer than year
sub_codes.description: Date of birth, admission date, exact event date.
sub_codes.movers: birth or incident dates raise risk; clinically meaningful timing raises nuance

example.text: It started right after the eleventh of March.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: the eleventh of March

sub_codes.name: Contact details
sub_codes.description: Phone number, email, social handle.
sub_codes.movers: fixed

example.text: You can reach me on the number ending in double four.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: the number ending in double four
example.after: You can reach me on my number.

sub_codes.name: Account or record number
sub_codes.description: Chart number, insurance number, government identifier, employee code.
sub_codes.movers: fixed

example.text: My file number here is 2291.
example.speaker: patient

cue_classes.name: Appearance and presentation
cue_classes.description: What the clinician observes in the first minutes, before any history is taken. Consistently reported as the first thing noticed.

sub_codes.name: Grooming or dress deviation
sub_codes.description: Dress or grooming departing from an implied norm. Note that the information sits in the comparison, not the observation, so simple redaction does not remove it.
sub_codes.movers: a distinctive personal style raises risk; first-session state observation raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: Unironed clothing and unmaintained hair described as a first-pass depression indicator.

example.text: Her clothes were creased and her hair had clearly not been combed for days.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: creased and her hair had clearly not been combed for days
example.rationale: High clinical value, low identifying power on its own. Only becomes risky inside a bundle.

sub_codes.name: Attire atypical for the setting
sub_codes.description: Uniform, occupational dress, religious dress, or anything unusual enough to prompt a question.
sub_codes.movers: visible insignia raises risk; pairing with APP-GROOM (a violated professional norm) raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: Clothing unusual enough that the clinician asked the patient about it directly.

example.text: He came to the OPD still in full uniform with his unit insignia visible.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: full uniform with his unit insignia visible
example.after: He came to the OPD still in his work uniform.

sub_codes.name: Distinguishing physical feature
sub_codes.description: Scar, visible disability, unusual build, distinctive marking.
sub_codes.movers: rarity of the feature raises risk; a feature tied to clinical history (self-harm) raises nuance sharply

example.text: There was a long burn scar running down the left side of his neck.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: long burn scar running down the left side of his neck
example.after: There was a visible old injury he seemed conscious of.

sub_codes.name: Observable affect at presentation
sub_codes.description: Crying, shivering, visible anxiety at first contact.
sub_codes.movers: near-universal; the trajectory across the session raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: Reported by three of five clinicians as a first-pass observation.

example.text: She was shivering slightly even before she sat down.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: shivering slightly even before she sat down

cue_classes.name: Demographic and role
cue_classes.description: Attributes that are individually weak and jointly strong. This class is the main source of bundle risk.

sub_codes.name: Age
sub_codes.description: Stated or inferred age. Clinicians use age to predict a typical presenting problem set, which is exactly the inference an attacker can also run.
sub_codes.movers: age extremes raise risk; bundling is what usually lifts it; life-stage relevance raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: One clinician described age 22 as predicting relationship, parental and uncertainty themes.

example.text: I am twenty-two, final year.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: twenty-two
example.after: I am in my early twenties, final year.
example.rationale: Kept at level 1 because developmental stage is clinically load-bearing. Escalates only if the bundle k_hat falls below tier.

sub_codes.name: Occupation, rank, employer, institution
sub_codes.description: The archetypal contextual identifier. Profession-linked bearing, vocabulary and institutional references survive name removal completely.
sub_codes.movers: niche, ranked or uniformed jobs raise risk; a job woven into the complaint (night shift + insomnia) raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: A serving military patient recalled primarily by occupational presentation rather than by clinical picture.

example.text: I am a junior commissioned officer, posted at a high-altitude station for the last two years.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: junior commissioned officer, posted at a high-altitude station
example.after: I am a non-commissioned officer at a remote posting, for the last two years.
example.rationale: Level 1 preserves the isolation and hierarchy pressure that make the posting clinically relevant.

sub_codes.name: Origin, residence, migration history
sub_codes.description: Highest external linkability of any class in the schema.
sub_codes.movers: a small place of origin raises risk; migration central to the case raises nuance

example.text: I moved here from a small town in the hills three years ago for the job.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: a small town in the hills
example.after: I moved here from another part of the country three years ago for the job.
example.rationale: Escalated to level 2 because this span sits in a bundle with DEM-OCC and DEM-AGE.

sub_codes.name: Family structure and marital status
sub_codes.description: Birth order, joint family configuration, marital status, number of children. Frequently high nuance.
sub_codes.movers: countable configurations (youngest of four) raise risk; family conflict as the presenting issue raises nuance

example.text: I am the youngest of four, and the only one who did not stay in the joint family house.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: the youngest of four, and the only one who did not stay in the joint family house
example.after: I am the youngest sibling, and the only one who moved out of the joint family house.
example.rationale: Exact sibling count removed; the position and the departure, which carry the clinical meaning, are kept.

sub_codes.name: Caste, community, religion, language group
sub_codes.description: Culturally load-bearing. Almost never suppress, because removing it can make the presenting conflict unintelligible.
sub_codes.movers: a tiny minority in that region raises risk; community pressure driving the case raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: Raised explicitly by one clinician as shaping the expected problem set alongside age.

example.text: The marriage was arranged within the community and refusing was not treated as an option.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: arranged within the community
example.rationale: Named community would be GENERALISE. An unnamed reference to community endogamy is common enough to keep, and the coercion dynamic is the clinical content.

sub_codes.name: Socioeconomic markers
sub_codes.description: Education level, housing type, income references, employment stability.
sub_codes.movers: precise markers raise risk; poverty or aspiration central to the case raises nuance

example.text: I am the first in my family to finish college.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: first in my family to finish college

sub_codes.name: Shared institutional setting
sub_codes.description: Hostel, campus, workplace or unit shared with the clinician. Enables dual-relationship identification, which no conventional identifier list covers.
sub_codes.movers: shared with the clinician starts high; the dual relationship as the clinical issue raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician described a patient living in the same hostel as her.

example.text: He was staying in the same hostel block as me, two floors down.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: same hostel block as me, two floors down
example.after: He lived in the same residential facility as me.
example.rationale: Floor-level detail suppressed; the dual relationship is retained because it is the clinical issue.

cue_classes.name: Narrative signature
cue_classes.description: Highest priority class. These are the cues clinicians actually recall a patient by, and they survive every conventional identifier pass untouched.

sub_codes.name: Patient-original phrasing
sub_codes.description: An idiom, metaphor or coinage the patient invented. The strongest single re-identification vector in the schema, and made worse by the professional convention of recording chief complaint as exact verbatim.

require: add nothing - a rewrite must never invent clinical content
rewrite_constraints.status: experiment-gated: the system proposes constrained rewrites; a human commits every one until feasibility is validated on synthetic coinages

sub_codes.movers: frequency-check singularity raises risk; the therapist actively using the phrase raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician recalled a patient's phrase about parents believing themselves infallible, remembered years later for its phrasing rather than its content.

example.text: My parents think they are gods, they cannot be wrong even once.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: My parents think they are gods
example.after: My parents act like they can never be wrong, not even once.
example.rationale: Constrained rewrite. Register, metaphor structure and emotional intensity preserved; the exact string is broken.
example.counter_example: Rewriting to 'my parents were controlling' would be a failure: correct in substance, but it destroys the register and the heat, which is the clinical signal.

sub_codes.name: Euphemism inviting a probe
sub_codes.description: A code word the patient introduces, often subconsciously, expecting the clinician to follow it.
sub_codes.movers: a private code word raises risk; a common cultural construction lowers it; hooks are nearly always nuance 3
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician described patients saying they are married and have a friend, a construction that on probing almost always discloses an affair.

example.text: I am married, and I also have a friend.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: I also have a friend
example.rationale: This particular hook is a recurring convention rather than an individual coinage, so it is common and therefore not identifying. It is tagged so the pipeline can distinguish shared hooks from individual coinages, which is exactly the distinction NAR-VERB needs.

sub_codes.name: Rare event or circumstance
sub_codes.description: An event, condition or life circumstance uncommon enough that it identifies by itself. Uniqueness relative to caseload is what makes clinicians remember it.

require: add nothing - a rewrite must never invent clinical content
rewrite_constraints.status: experiment-gated: the system proposes constrained rewrites; a human commits every one until feasibility is validated on synthetic coinages

sub_codes.movers: an event famous in a community raises risk sharply; index trauma raises nuance, an incidental event lowers it
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician recalled a case remembered specifically because the underlying condition was unique in her experience.

example.text: The whole thing started after the factory fire, when I was the only one who got out of that shift.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: after the factory fire, when I was the only one who got out of that shift
example.after: It started after an accident at work, where I was the only survivor among the people around me.
example.rationale: Sole-survivor guilt is the clinical content and must survive. The specific reportable event is removed because it is externally searchable.

sub_codes.name: Identifying fragment about a third party
sub_codes.description: The detail that pinpoints another person: a name, workplace, school, precise location. Never the relational content itself — that is KEEP-REL; hybrids stack KEEP-REL over the sentence with NAR-THIRD on the fragment. Treatment ranges by the fragment's meaning: nuance 3 function-preserving blur, nuance 2 swap, nuance 0-1 replace with a smoothing bridge. Deleting details never deletes the person — coreference keeps every character in the story. These people did not consent to anything.
sub_codes.movers: identifying precision about the other person raises risk; case-relevance raises nuance - delete only at nuance 0-1

example.text: My wife teaches at the girls' school behind the bus depot.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: teaches at the girls' school behind the bus depot

sub_codes.name: Temporal anchor to a public event
sub_codes.description: A datable public event used to place the narrative in time.
sub_codes.movers: newsworthy, datable anchors raise risk; timing-as-cause raises nuance

example.text: It began during the lockdown, right when the board exams were cancelled.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: during the lockdown, right when the board exams were cancelled
example.after: It began during a period when my exams were disrupted.
example.rationale: The disruption is the clinical content. The datable anchor narrows the cohort and is removed.

sub_codes.name: Cultural idiom of distress
sub_codes.description: A culturally specific way of expressing suffering or hopelessness. High nuance, moderate risk. Generalise carefully or the transcript stops sounding like a real person.

require: break the exact string only when the idiom is hyper-local
add nothing - a rewrite must never invent clinical content
rewrite_constraints.status: experiment-gated: the system proposes constrained rewrites; a human commits every one until feasibility is validated on synthetic coinages

sub_codes.movers: a hyper-local idiom raises risk; voice authenticity raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician noted that a resigned, casual remark about medication being pointless stayed with her precisely because of how it was said.

example.text: Medicine leke bhi kya ho jayega, it is all the same anyway.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: Medicine leke bhi kya ho jayega
example.rationale: Shared cultural idiom, not an individual coinage. Removing it would strip the hopelessness marker and the code-mixing that makes the transcript authentic.

cue_classes.name: Paralinguistic and nonverbal
cue_classes.description: Near-universal individually and therefore almost never identifying on their own. Annotators should resist marking them as risky. They are tagged because bundle linking needs them to construct bindings.

sub_codes.name: Body language
sub_codes.description: Fidgeting, arm crossing, gaze aversion, closed posture, looking away.
sub_codes.movers: alone near-worthless; its value is as a binding ingredient
sub_codes.interview_basis: All five clinicians converged on this set.

example.text: She kept her arms crossed for most of the first half.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: kept her arms crossed

sub_codes.name: Paralinguistic features
sub_codes.description: Volume, pitch, pace, stutter, and change over the session. The trajectory carries more information than the state.
sub_codes.movers: a highly distinctive described pattern raises risk; change over the session raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician described tracking stutter onset at the start and how it eased as rapport built.

example.text: He stammered badly for the first ten minutes and then it settled almost completely.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: stammered badly for the first ten minutes and then it settled
example.rationale: A persistent, severe speech characteristic would score higher. A transient anxiety stammer that resolves is common.

sub_codes.name: Meaningful silence
sub_codes.description: A pause carrying content, including the silence of realisation.
sub_codes.movers: never identifying alone

example.text: She went completely quiet for about half a minute, and then said she had never put it that way before.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: went completely quiet for about half a minute

sub_codes.name: Language switching
sub_codes.description: Code-switching: the speaker changes language or slips into their mother tongue mid-conversation. Near-universal in code-mixed speech, and behaves like silence: individually harmless, tagged as raw material for bindings - a switch that clusters at one specific topic is a tell.
sub_codes.movers: a highly distinctive personal switching pattern raises risk slightly; a switch bound to one topic moves the risk into the NVB-BOUND composite, not this span

example.text: We discussed the wedding calmly in English, but the moment her mother came up she said, 'Woh samjhengi nahin, doctor. Kabhi nahin.'
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: the moment her mother came up she said, 'Woh samjhengi nahin, doctor. Kabhi nahin.'
example.rationale: Switching to the mother tongue is common and identifies no one. What matters is the pattern: if the switch happens only when the mother is raised, the binding engine fuses switch and topic into an NVB-BOUND composite, and that composite carries the risk.

sub_codes.name: Cue-topic binding
sub_codes.description: A composite span generated at the bundle-linking stage when a marker-capable cue (any code flagged marker_capable — nonverbal or not: silence, stutter, gaze, deflection, language switch) occurs at a specific topic and not at the session baseline. This is the only NVB code that is usually identifying.
sub_codes.binding_rule: bind(marker, topic) iff |pos(marker) - pos(topic)| < window AND P(marker | topic) / P(marker | baseline) > lift_threshold. The parameters (window, lift_threshold) are tunables and live in the policy file (anonymization-policy.json), set per marker type and adjusted from test runs.
sub_codes.movers: lift over the session baseline raises risk; what the topic is raises nuance

example.text: He was fine throughout, but every time his elder brother came up he stopped making eye contact.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: every time his elder brother came up he stopped making eye contact
example.after: Every time a particular family member came up he stopped making eye contact.
example.rationale: Gaze aversion alone is risk 0. Bound to one named relation it becomes a recognition cue, so the relation is generalised while the binding itself is kept.

cue_classes.name: Interactional dynamics
cue_classes.description: Behaviour during rupture and resistance. The behaviour is generic; what triggered it usually is not.

sub_codes.name: Resistance behaviour
sub_codes.description: Avoidance, zoning out, deflection to an unrelated topic, direct refusal, stock non-answers, speeding up.
sub_codes.movers: the behaviour is generic; the trigger (via binding) is where risk hides
sub_codes.interview_basis: Two clinicians independently listed avoidance, zoning out, topic shifting, refusal, fidgeting and silence.

example.text: Every time I asked, the answer was just I don't know, and then he changed the subject.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: just I don't know, and then he changed the subject

sub_codes.name: Confrontation or rupture
sub_codes.description: An explicit challenge, whether patient or clinician initiated, including confrontation used deliberately as technique.
sub_codes.movers: quoted unusual confrontations raise risk; rupture-and-repair raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician described using gentle confrontation to surface a contradiction from a previous session.

example.text: I said, that isn't quite what you told me last week, is it?
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: that isn't quite what you told me last week, is it?
example.rationale: Clinician technique, high research value, no identifying content.

sub_codes.name: Boundary incident
sub_codes.description: A demand outside the therapeutic frame, a threat, or retaliation following a refusal. High risk because incidents are memorable and often documented elsewhere.
sub_codes.movers: incidents documented elsewhere (complaints) raise risk sharply
sub_codes.interview_basis: A clinician described a patient demanding an unscheduled session and threatening to retaliate when refused.

example.text: When I said we would keep to the scheduled time, he told me he would make sure I regretted it.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: he told me he would make sure I regretted it
example.after: When I held to the scheduled time, he responded with a threat.
example.rationale: The dynamic is retained. Specific wording removed because an incident of this kind is likely recorded elsewhere and therefore cross-linkable.

sub_codes.name: Dual relationship
sub_codes.description: Clinician and patient share a social or institutional context outside the session. Pairs with DEM-SETTING in a bundle.
sub_codes.movers: specificity of the shared context raises risk; usually the clinical issue itself, so nuance 3

example.text: I knew him socially before he ever became a patient, which made all of this harder.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: knew him socially before he ever became a patient
example.rationale: Kept because the dual relationship is the clinical issue. Risk is carried by the paired DEM-SETTING span, which is generalised instead.

sub_codes.name: Turning point
sub_codes.description: The moment the clinician still pictures clearly. Clinician-recall salience is a usable proxy for distinctiveness.
sub_codes.movers: memorable is not identifying, unless the moment involves a rare event

example.text: The moment everything changed was when he finally looked up and said he had never told anyone.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: finally looked up and said he had never told anyone
example.rationale: Salient to the clinician but not distinctive across patients. Risk rises only if the disclosure content itself is rare.

cue_classes.name: Clinician-side signals
cue_classes.description: These identify the therapist, not only the patient. A corpus that protects patients while exposing clinician behaviour to their employer has traded one privacy problem for another. Expect low yield from interviews, since clinicians asked about their own bias answer with protocol rather than incident.

sub_codes.name: Countertransference marker
sub_codes.description: Evaluative adjectives, unusual warmth or distance, moralising, or a register shift specific to one patient.
sub_codes.movers: institutional readership raises risk - third-lever territory

example.text: Honestly this one was just an entitled kid, and I could feel myself getting short with him.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: just an entitled kid, and I could feel myself getting short with him

annotation.notes: flag for clinician-consent tier rather than transform

example.after: unchanged in the research tier; withheld from any release visible to the clinician's employer
example.rationale: Transforming this destroys the phenomenon the class exists to study. The correct control is access, not rewriting.

sub_codes.name: Clinician self-disclosure
sub_codes.description: The clinician offering information about their own life or reactions.
sub_codes.movers: specific biography raises risk; disclosure-as-technique raises nuance

example.text: I told her I had been through something similar during my own training years.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: I had been through something similar during my own training years
example.after: I told her I had been through something similar myself.

sub_codes.name: Supervision or referral reference
sub_codes.description: Mention of supervision, a named colleague, or an onward referral decision.
sub_codes.movers: named colleagues or units raise risk
sub_codes.interview_basis: Clinicians described referring cases outside their specialisation to a better-suited colleague.

example.text: I felt this was outside what I handle, so I passed it to the OCD clinic upstairs.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: the OCD clinic upstairs
example.after: I felt this was outside what I handle, so I referred it to a specialist service.

sub_codes.name: Humour or informal register as technique
sub_codes.description: Deliberate informality used to open a patient up.
sub_codes.movers: quoted running jokes raise risk slightly; technique value raises nuance
sub_codes.interview_basis: One clinician described humour as her main tool for getting patients to open up.

example.text: I laughed and said we would both pretend I hadn't noticed that.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: we would both pretend I hadn't noticed that
example.rationale: A distinctive personal style is a clinician fingerprint, but it is also the procedural knowledge research most wants. Handle by access tier, not transformation.

cue_classes.name: Preserve class
cue_classes.description: The negative class. Annotated as diligently as the risky classes, because a model trained only on positive spans learns to over-redact.

sub_codes.name: Symptom description
sub_codes.description: Symptom content with no identifying specificity.
sub_codes.movers: risk above 0 means the label is wrong - re-code, do not treat

example.text: I have no energy for anything, and nothing feels interesting any more.
example.speaker: patient
example.span: no energy for anything, and nothing feels interesting any more

sub_codes.name: Affect trajectory
sub_codes.description: How affect moves across the session.
sub_codes.movers: risk above 0 means the label is wrong - re-code, do not treat

example.text: She started guarded and by the end was answering in full paragraphs.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: started guarded and by the end was answering in full paragraphs

sub_codes.name: Therapeutic move
sub_codes.description: Reflection, reframe, deliberate silence, offering a tissue or water, permission to defer a question. The procedural knowledge most downstream research wants.
sub_codes.movers: risk above 0 means the label is wrong - re-code, do not treat
sub_codes.interview_basis: Multiple clinicians described the same de-escalation sequence: offer a tissue, hold the silence, invite them to continue when ready.

example.text: I offered her a tissue, sat with the silence, and told her we could pick it up whenever she was ready.
example.speaker: clinician
example.span: offered her a tissue, sat with the silence, and told her we could pick it up whenever she was ready

sub_codes.name: Cultural or religious content
sub_codes.description: Cultural or religious material with no linkage value.
sub_codes.movers: risk above 0 means the label is wrong - re-code, do not treat

example.text: I still do the morning prayer, it is the only part of the day that feels steady.

sub_codes.description: What the people around the speaker do to or with them — conflict, support, pressure, neglect — with no identifying specificity. The cargo layer of third-party content; any identifying fragment riding inside it is stacked as a secondary NAR-THIRD span and treated on its own.

generalisation_hierarchies._note: These chains are few-shot exemplars showing how WE do generalisation: small steps, minimum rungs, meaning preserved. They are not lookup tables. Generalisations are generated per instance, guided by these exemplars, and every candidate passes the standard gates (meaning floor, risk re-check). A new chain is authored only when test runs show a class generalising badly.

example_chain: a junior commissioned officer posted at a high-altitude border station
a non-commissioned officer at a remote posting
a serving soldier in a demanding posting
a person in a disciplined uniformed profession
DEM-OCC.guidance: Climb the minimum number of levels that brings the bundle k_hat above the tier threshold, and no further. Level 1 usually preserves everything clinically relevant.

bundle_examples.rationale: Age band plus a specific posting type plus region of origin. Each span alone scores 1 to 2. Together they narrow the population to single digits, which is the failure mode a per-span scorer misses entirely.
A shared residential setting plus a documented boundary incident. Anyone in that institution at that time could identify both parties.
Gaze aversion is universal. Gaze aversion occurring only at one named relation is a recognition cue for anyone who knows the family.

annotator_rules: Read the whole transcript before annotating anything. Bundle risk cannot be judged utterance by utterance.
Tag the KEEP class as diligently as the risky classes.
Unsure between risk 2 and risk 3? Ask whether someone who already knows this patient could recognise them from this span alone. If yes, it is 3.
Unsure about nuance? Ask whether the clinical story still makes sense to a supervisor with the span deleted. If not, it is 3.
Do not resolve the action yourself when risk and nuance are both 3. Flag it for adjudication.
Never assign SUPPRESS to a span with nuance 2 or 3. SUPPRESS is permitted only at nuance 0 or 1. Anything above that is a system error, not a judgement call.
